title: Switchboards: Please Hold While We Connect You
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Kyle's research input) explore the history of the telephone switchboard: Alexander Graham Bell's telephone and early Bell Telephone Company, the first commercial switchboard in New Haven in 1878, the switchboard problem and divided and Express systems, the early long-distance chain of town switchboards and the 1915 New York to San Francisco call, Bell-era monopoly tactics, phone numbering from exchange names like Klondike 5 to all-numeric numbers, the female "Hello girls" operators and their strict working conditions and strikes, Strowger's automatic switch and rotary dial pulses, and the last manual switchboards such as Bryant Pond, Maine and Kerman, California. Ends with a listener mail follow-up about Joe Theismann's surname pronunciation.
topics: New York to San Francisco 1915 call

segments.title: Opening banter and telephone museum
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of telephone switchboards, mention a telephone museum in Maitland, Florida, and discuss whether landlines still have any purpose such as home alarm systems.

segments.title: Bell's telephone and the origins of the switchboard
segments.summary: Bell patented the telephone in 1876 while trying to solve telegraph congestion; the first permanent wires were set up in Boston and a Bell company was founded the next year. Direct point-to-point wiring became unmanageable, leading to the central switchboard concept.

segments.title: First commercial switchboard and early operator service
segments.summary: The first commercial switchboard opened in New Haven, Connecticut in 1878 with 21 subscribers. Early operators connected calls by name, announced callers, and tracked calls for billing. Phone numbers were not yet used.

segments.title: Phone growth and telephone costs
segments.summary: Telephone subscribers grew rapidly from about 60,000 to 260,000 and then to three million in the US, with the UK lagging behind until catching up. Phone companies rented phones to customers and controlled the equipment.

segments.title: Switchboard problem and divided exchange
segments.summary: As subscribers multiplied, switchboards became crowded and the so-called switchboard problem arose. Solutions included the divided exchange, which specialized operator roles, and the Express system with A and B boards linked by operators. Improved signal lamps and centralized power helped.
topics: Express system A board B board

segments.title: Isolated town telephone systems
segments.summary: Phone systems were largely internal to each town, and long-distance connections were not yet available between major cities such as New York and San Francisco.
topics: New York to San Francisco no connection

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break with hosts joking about the word stuck.

segments.title: Long-distance calls through chained switchboards
segments.summary: Long-distance calls were relayed by human operators passing connections switchboard to switchboard through trunk lines. The first long line linked New York and Philadelphia, New York to San Francisco arrived in 1915, and Bell was brought out for the call.

segments.title: Bell monopoly and patent lawsuits
segments.summary: Bell used lawsuits, detectives, and bribery against competitors during the patent period and after. Bell Telephone bought AT&T and consolidated the industry under JP Morgan's influence. A government-sanctioned monopoly lasted for decades before a breakup. AT&T was tasked with long distance lines to control the market.

segments.title: Telephone numbers and exchange names
segments.summary: Early numbers were short and town-based. Exchange names like Klondike were later combined with digits, then letters were replaced by numbers, leading to all-number dialing, and eventually area codes and ten-digit numbers. The 555 exchange was reserved for fictional movie phone numbers.

segments.title: Hello girls and the work of switchboard operators
segments.summary: Teenage boys were tried first but gave customers back as good as they got, so most operators became women. Emma Nutt was the first hired, in 1878. Operators needed to be well spoken, educated, and of good character, and jobs were limited for women. Bell's booklet discouraged saying hello, and the hello versus hoy debate is recounted.

segments.title: Operator working conditions and strikes
segments.summary: Supervisors closely monitored operators, who faced harsh discipline. Customers made abusive or trivial requests. Operators were limited to a few scripted phrases, and New England telephone operators went on strike in 1919 over union recognition.

segments.title: Women operators in World War I
segments.summary: Two hundred twenty-three American women served as bilingual switchboard operators in Europe for the US Army Signal Corps during World War I because France's phone system was damaged. They were recognized as veterans in 1979.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the discussion of automation.

segments.title: Automation: rotary dial and Strowger switch
segments.summary: Numeric numbering made automation possible. Rotary dials sent electrical pulses matching each digit as the dial returned. Almon Brown Strowger, an undertaker in Kansas City, invented the automatic switch in 1890 after losing business to a rival whose wife was the town operator. The switch narrowed connections digit by digit.

segments.title: End of operators and last manual switchboards
segments.summary: Cost drove automation. Long-distance switching stayed manual into the late 1960s and 1970s because it was complex. Operators knew complex routing. By the 1970s the system was digitized, though some small switchboards persisted. Notable last manual systems include Bryant Pond, Maine (1983, hand-cranked), a UK exchange, and a Kerman, California company whose bilingual operators served Spanish-speaking customers.

segments.title: Listener mail: Joe Theismann surname pronunciation
segments.summary: A listener follow-up says former Washington football quarterback Joe Theismann's family pronounced their name 'Thighs-man', as confirmed by a story Joe told at a conference.
